life-vitc-cold: The evidence that it prevents colds is weak — getting your daily amount from food (**40 mg** for adults) is enough. Your body can't store vitamin C, so whatever you don't use leaves in your urine. Taking more than 1,000 mg a day as a supplement can cause stomach pain and diarrhea. Handwashing, sleep and fluids do more to prevent colds. If you catch one, rest and drink plenty of fluids, and see a doctor if a fever lasts more than three days.
life-vitc: Adults need **40 mg** a day, and taking more doesn't make it work better. Your body can't store vitamin C, so the extra leaves in your urine — two tangerines cover a day's worth. Supplements over **1,000 mg** a day can cause stomach pain, diarrhea or gas, which usually stop when you stop taking them. Get it from fruit and vegetables, and if you take a supplement, you could choose one under 1,000 mg. If you've had kidney stones or have kidney problems, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before taking high doses.
life-vitd: How much vitamin D should I take a day?

For most people, **10 micrograms (400 IU)** a day is enough. Your skin makes it in sunlight, but in winter or if you rarely go outside you can run low. Adults shouldn't go over **100 micrograms (4,000 IU)** a day; for children aged 1 to 10 the upper limit is 50 micrograms (2,000 IU). Multivitamins and calcium products also contain vitamin D, so add them all up. If you've had a bone injection or a high-dose prescription, check with your prescriber before buying more.
life-vita: Is it OK to take vitamin A supplements for a long time?

It's best to keep vitamin A from food and supplements combined under **1.5 mg** a day. Research suggests that more than this over many years may make bones more likely to break later in life. If you eat liver more than once a week, you could drop supplements that contain vitamin A (including fish liver oil). Women after menopause and older men should be especially careful to stay under this limit. If you're pregnant, talk to your doctor before eating liver or taking vitamin A supplements.
life-iron: How much iron supplement is safe?

Iron supplements of **17 mg** a day or less usually cause no problems. Over **20 mg**, constipation, nausea and stomach pain are common, and very high amounts are especially dangerous for children. Iron tablets can look like candy, so the most important thing is to keep them out of children's reach. If heavy periods leave you tired, a blood test for anemia before increasing supplements may be a good idea. If a child swallows iron tablets — any number — call 119 right away.
life-calcium: Will more calcium make my bones stronger?

Adults need **700 mg** a day, and milk, cheese, tofu and fish eaten with the bones cover most of it. Spinach has a lot of calcium, but the body can't absorb all of it. Supplements over **1,500 mg** a day can cause stomach pain and diarrhea. It's best to take calcium at a different time from iron and thyroid medicine. If you take osteoporosis medicine, ask your prescriber how much calcium to add.
life-zinc: Can I take zinc supplements for a long time?

Unless a doctor advised it, it's best not to take more than **25 mg** of zinc supplements a day. Taking a lot of zinc makes your body absorb less copper. Cold remedies with zinc, multivitamins and immune gummies often overlap, so add them all up. Meat, shellfish and nuts can also cover your daily amount. If you develop tingling in your hands and feet or anemia after taking it for a long time, tell your doctor you take zinc.
life-magnesium: Supplements over **400 mg** a day can cause diarrhea. Magnesium draws water into the gut — the same ingredient is used as a laxative. Spinach, nuts and wholegrain bread also contain it, so food can cover it too. If you get diarrhea, try a smaller dose or split it up. If you have kidney problems, magnesium can build up in the body, so talk to a doctor or pharmacist first.
life-stack: Can I take several supplements together?

Often you can, but first look for **the same ingredient adding up too much**. A single multivitamin often already contains vitamin D, zinc and vitamin A, so combined with separate products it's easy to go over the upper limit. Gather the labels and add up each ingredient's daily amount to see the overlaps. If you put your supplements in My medicines too, you can see overlaps with your medicines as well. If you take medicines, bring the bottles to your pharmacist and ask, “Does anything overlap with my medicines?”
life-vitb-pee: Vitamin B turns my urine yellow — is that OK?

Bright yellow urine from vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is common and harmless. It's the color of leftover vitamin B2 leaving your body in urine. Since the extra just leaves, high-dose products aren't necessarily better. Drinking plenty of water makes the color lighter. If your urine is dark brown after stopping the supplement, or your eyes or skin turn yellow, see a doctor.
life-broccoli: Is broccoli really good for you?

Yes — but eating **a variety of vegetables** matters more than any single ‘superfood’. Broccoli is one of the vegetables richest in vitamin C, and one serving nearly covers a day's worth. Aim for fruit and vegetables five times a day, **80 g** each time (about two large florets of broccoli). Blanching or steaming keeps more of the vitamins. If you take warfarin, don't suddenly eat much more or less green vegetables — keep it steady.
life-fruitveg: How much fruit and vegetables should I eat a day?

The goal is **five times a day**, **80 g** each time. An apple, a banana or two broccoli florets each count as one. Dried fruit counts as one at **30 g**, and potatoes count as a starch, not a vegetable. Frozen and canned vegetables count too — choose ones without added sugar or salt. If you've been told to cut down on potassium because of your kidneys, follow your care team on fruit amounts.
life-water: How much water should I drink a day?

The guide is **6–8 cups** a day, and if your urine is **clear and pale yellow**, you're drinking enough. Milk, tea and coffee count toward this too, not just water. You need more when it's hot, when you exercise for a long time, when you're ill, or when pregnant or breastfeeding. Try spreading it through the day before you feel thirsty. If you've been told to limit fluids because of your heart or kidneys, follow that amount.
life-salt: How much salt is too much a day?

For adults the guide is **5 g of salt or less** a day (2,000 mg of sodium · about one teaspoon) — the Korean Society of Hypertension lowered it from 6 g to 5 g in its 2026 6th edition, matching the World Health Organization. Korean adults eat about **8 g** a day on average, roughly 1.6 times the recommendation — most of it is already in soups, kimchi and noodles. Try leaving half the soup and seasoning with garlic, pepper or lemon instead of salt. Multiply the sodium on a nutrition label by 2.5 to get the amount of salt. If you take blood pressure medicine, the less salt you eat, the better it works — show your blood pressure log at your visit.
life-walk: How much exercise do I need?

Adults should aim for **150 minutes** a week (30 minutes on five days) of activity that makes you a little out of breath. Brisk walking is enough, and if the exercise makes you very out of breath, 75 minutes gives a similar benefit. Add **two days** a week of exercises that work your legs, back and arms. If you're just starting, you could begin with 10-minute chunks. If your chest tightens or you get very short of breath while walking, stop and see a doctor.
life-sleep: Should I take medicine first when I can't sleep?

Adults usually need **7–9 hours**, and changing sleep habits comes before medicine. Pharmacy sleep aids can't fix sleep and only help for about 1–2 weeks. Go to bed only when sleepy, get up at the same time every day, and put screens away an hour before bed. Cutting naps and late-afternoon coffee deepens night sleep. If months of poor sleep make daytime hard, see a doctor — there are treatments without medicine.
life-cold-abx: Do antibiotics help a cold get better faster?

No — colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics don't work on them. Taking antibiotics when you don't need them can make them stop working when you really do. A cold usually gets better on its own in **1–2 weeks**. Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and ease fever and aches with a fever reducer. See a doctor if a fever lasts more than three days or you get short of breath.
life-cold-when: When should I see a doctor for a cold?

Most colds get better at home in 1–2 weeks. But see a doctor if a fever lasts **more than three days**, symptoms keep getting worse, or you get short of breath or chest pain. If you have diabetes, heart or lung disease, or are on cancer treatment, it's better to go early. Until then, rest, drink plenty of fluids, and check ingredients so you don't double up a fever reducer with a combination cold medicine. If you're gasping or your lips turn blue, call 119 right away.
life-cough-3w: My cough won't go away — when should I see a doctor?

A cough usually stops on its own within **3–4 weeks**. See a doctor if it lasts **more than 3 weeks**, you lose weight for no reason, or your immune system is weak from cancer treatment, diabetes and so on. Meanwhile rest, drink plenty of fluids, and you could try honey in warm water (no honey for babies under 1). If you cough up phlegm with blood, don't wait — see a doctor. If you're too short of breath to finish a sentence, call 119.
life-throat-week: My throat hurts — when should I see a doctor?

A sore throat usually gets better within **a week**, and antibiotics are rarely needed. Gargle with warm salt water (not for children), sip water often, and eat cool or soft foods. See a doctor if it hasn't improved after a week, keeps coming back, or the child is under 5. If someone can't swallow and drools, or struggles to breathe, call 119 right away.
life-fever-adult: At what temperature is it a fever in adults?

Usually **38 °C or above** counts as a fever. A fever is a sign your body is fighting germs, so look at how you feel, not just the number. Rest, drink enough that your urine is pale yellow, and take a fever reducer if you're uncomfortable. If it isn't getting better or keeps getting worse after caring for it at home, see a doctor. If you're on cancer treatment, don't wait from 38 °C — contact your treating hospital right away.
life-diarrhea-sip: What should I eat and drink with diarrhea?

The most important thing is to drink **small sips often**. If you can't replace the fluid lost through diarrhea, you'll feel dizzy and pass less urine. If you feel sick, take one sip at a time, and keep giving babies breast milk or formula in small, frequent feeds. Washing hands with soap often helps stop it spreading to your family. If you vomit something like coffee grounds, have bloody stools with a fever, or barely pass urine, see a doctor right away.
life-constip-life: Is there anything besides medicine for constipation?

First try increasing three things: **fiber, fluids and movement**. Fruits like apples, apricots, grapes and strawberries, plus oats and whole grains, soften stools. Increase fiber slowly, since a sudden jump can upset your stomach, and don't hold it in when you feel the urge. If that doesn't work, pharmacy laxatives usually work within three days. If there's blood in your stool or it lasts for weeks, see a doctor.
life-honey-baby: Give honey only **after the first birthday (12 months)**. Bacterial spores in honey can make toxins in a baby's gut before age one. Even if you want to give honey water for a cough, don't before age one. Children over one and adults can soothe a throat with honey in warm water. If a baby under one becomes badly constipated, weak or feeds poorly after eating honey, see a doctor right away.
life-cold-dup: Can I take a combination cold medicine with a fever reducer?

Better not to take them separately — combination cold medicines often already contain a fever reducer/pain reliever. Getting the same ingredient twice makes it easy to go over the daily limit. First check the box for acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Enter both medicine names in Yakjido to see right away if they overlap. If you're unsure, show both boxes to your pharmacist and ask, “Do these have the same ingredient?”
life-nasal-spray: Can I keep using a decongestant nasal spray?

Decongestant sprays (like xylometazoline) are for short use — **within three days**. Using them longer can make your nose more blocked when you stop, so the approved label also says not to use them for more than **7 days** in a row (up to 3 times a day). Cold congestion usually clears in 1–2 weeks even without a spray, so use it only when really blocked (like at bedtime). If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, diabetes, glaucoma or an enlarged prostate, tell your pharmacist before using it. If it isn't better after three days of use, see a doctor.
life-shampoo: Is sulfate-free shampoo good for hair loss?

It may be gentler for a sensitive scalp, but **there's little evidence it prevents hair loss.** Hair naturally falls out a little every day, and it often sheds more for a while after stress, illness, weight loss or low iron, then grows back. Choose a shampoo that suits your scalp, and if hair loss worries you, look for the cause first. Hair loss medicines only work while you use them. If hair falls out in round patches or you're worried, see a doctor.
life-hair-fall: My hair is suddenly falling out a lot

Most of the time it **falls out for a while and then grows back.** It's common to shed a lot all at once a few months after a major illness, stress, big weight loss or low iron. Once the cause passes, it usually grows back. If you also feel tired and dizzy, a blood test for anemia may be a good idea. If hair falls out in round patches, your scalp is itchy and red, or you're worried, see a doctor.
life-flu-when: When should I see a doctor for the flu?

Healthy adults usually recover in about a week. See a doctor quickly if you're **65 or older**, pregnant or recently gave birth, have diabetes, heart or lung disease, or you're worried about a child. At home, rest, drink plenty of fluids, and make sure your fever reducer and flu remedy don't share an ingredient. As with colds, antibiotics don't work for flu. If you suddenly get chest pain, become very short of breath, or cough up blood, call 119 right away.
life-when-er: Do I really need to go to the hospital?

If any of these apply, don't wait — call **119**: crushing chest pain, too short of breath to finish a sentence, weakness on one side or slurred speech, hard to wake, vomiting blood or something like coffee grounds. Without these signs, most things can be watched at home. See a doctor if a fever lasts **three days**, a cough **3 weeks**, or a sore throat **a week**. For older adults, pregnancy, cancer treatment or babies, go sooner. If unsure, check that symptom's warning signs under ‘Pick what's bothering you’ in Yakjido.
life-hives-worry: Hives — worried it might be HIV, scabies or a fungal infection?

Each raised welt of hives usually fades **within 24 hours** and new ones appear elsewhere — moving around within hours is the key feature. A rash from acute HIV infection comes about **2–4 weeks** (up to 6) after exposure together with flu-like symptoms such as fever, sore throat and swollen glands, and it doesn't move around within hours. But these flu-like symptoms also come with common illnesses, so you can't tell by appearance alone — if you're worried about an exposure, **testing** is the way to know regardless of the rash, and **within 72 hours** ask an emergency department or infectious disease clinic right away whether you can get preventive medicine. Scabies is marked by **itching that's worse at night** and thin lines between the fingers or on the wrists, and the rash can take up to **8 weeks** to appear after catching it. A fungal infection (ringworm) is a **ring** with a red edge that grows slowly and doesn't move around. Photos of the same spot taken a few hours apart help a lot at your visit, and if your lips, tongue or throat swell or you're short of breath, call 119 without waiting to check the shape.
